notes.definition: A magnetic field is the region around a magnet where a force acts on another magnet or on a magnetic material (iron, steel, cobalt and nickel). Field lines show the direction of the force on a north pole: from the north pole of a magnet to the south pole.
explanation: A magnetic field is the region around a magnet in which a force acts on another magnet or on a magnetic material. The magnetic materials are iron, steel, cobalt and nickel. The force between a magnet and a magnetic material is always one of attraction. Magnetic fields cannot be seen, so we represent them with magnetic field lines.

The direction of the magnetic field at any point is the direction of the force that would act on a north pole placed at that point. Because a north pole is repelled by a north pole and attracted to a south pole, the field lines always point away from the north pole of a magnet and towards its south pole. Arrows are drawn on field lines to show this direction. Field lines never cross.

The strength of a magnetic field depends on the distance from the magnet. The field is strongest at the poles and gets weaker further away. On a field diagram, the closer together the field lines are, the stronger the field. Around a bar magnet the lines are crowded together near the poles and spread out further away, showing how the strength changes.

A magnetic compass contains a small bar magnet, the needle, which is free to turn. The needle lines up with the magnetic field, and its north pole points in the direction of the field. To plot the field of a bar magnet, place the magnet on paper, put a plotting compass near the north pole and mark a dot at the tip of the needle. Move the compass so its tail is on that dot, mark the new tip, and repeat until you reach the south pole. Join the dots and add an arrow. Repeat starting at different points to build up the pattern.

Away from any other magnet, a compass needle points north. This is evidence that the Earth has its own magnetic field, which behaves as if there were a giant bar magnet inside the Earth. The Earth's core is magnetic. Because the north pole of a compass is attracted towards the geographic North Pole, the Earth's magnetic pole near the geographic North Pole is actually a magnetic south pole.
keyFacts: A magnetic field is the region around a magnet where a force acts on another magnet or a magnetic material.
Magnetic materials are iron, steel, cobalt and nickel.
The force between a magnet and a magnetic material is always attraction.
Field direction is the direction of the force on a north pole placed at that point.
Field lines go from the north pole to the south pole of a magnet.
The field is strongest at the poles and weaker further from the magnet.
Closer field lines mean a stronger field; field lines never cross.
A compass contains a small bar magnet that points in the direction of the Earth's magnetic field.
A compass pointing north when away from magnets is evidence that the Earth's core is magnetic.

keyTerms.definition: The region around a magnet where a force acts on another magnet or on a magnetic material.
A line showing the direction of the force on a north pole at each point; arrows point from N to S.
How strong the magnetic force is at a point; shown by how close together the field lines are.
A small compass whose needle (a tiny bar magnet) lines up with a magnetic field, used to map field lines.
The magnetic field produced by the Earth's core, which makes compass needles point north.
A material attracted by a magnet: iron, steel, cobalt or nickel.

workedExamples.title: Reading a field diagram
workedExamples.question: Point P is close to the north pole of a bar magnet, where field lines are close together. Point Q is far from the magnet, where lines are spread out. At which point is the field stronger, and which way does a compass needle point at P?
steps: Field lines closer together mean a stronger field, so the field is stronger at P.
Field lines leave the north pole, so at P the field points away from the north pole.
The compass needle's north pole points along the field.
workedExamples.answer: The field is stronger at P, and the compass needle at P points away from the magnet's north pole.

workedExamples.title: Plotting a field line
workedExamples.question: Describe how to use a plotting compass to draw one field line of a bar magnet.
steps: Place the magnet on paper and draw round it; label N and S.
Put the compass near the N pole and mark a dot at the end of the needle's north pole.
Move the compass so the tail of the needle is over the dot and mark a new dot at the tip.
Repeat until the compass reaches the S pole, then join the dots with a smooth curve and add an arrow from N to S.
workedExamples.answer: A sequence of dots joined into a smooth curve, from N to S, with an arrow showing direction.

workedExamples.title: Explaining the Earth's field
workedExamples.question: A compass is taken far from any magnets or iron objects. Its north pole always points to the north. Explain what this tells us about the Earth.
steps: A compass needle is a magnet that lines up with a magnetic field.
It lines up even with no magnet nearby, so the Earth must have a magnetic field.
This field comes from the Earth's core, which is magnetic.
workedExamples.answer: The Earth has its own magnetic field, so its core must be magnetic.

misconceptions.wrong: Students often draw field lines going from south to north outside a magnet.
misconceptions.right: In fact field lines point away from the north pole and towards the south pole, because they show the direction of the force on a north pole.

misconceptions.wrong: Students often think a field line shows a path that the magnetic force travels along.
misconceptions.right: In fact a field line shows the direction of the force on a north pole at each point; the closeness of the lines shows the field strength.

misconceptions.wrong: Students often think the Earth's magnetic pole near the geographic North Pole is a magnetic north pole.
misconceptions.right: In fact it is a magnetic south pole, because it attracts the north pole of a compass needle.

misconceptions.wrong: Students often think field lines can cross.
misconceptions.right: In fact field lines never cross, because the field can only have one direction at each point.

realWorld: Navigators and hikers use compasses, which line up with the Earth's magnetic field, to find north.
The Earth's magnetic field deflects charged particles from the Sun; where they reach the atmosphere near the poles they produce aurorae.
Some animals, including migrating birds and turtles, are thought to use the Earth's magnetic field to navigate.
examTips: When drawing a field pattern, always add arrows from N to S, draw smooth lines that never cross and draw the lines closer together near the poles.
When asked how field strength changes, say it decreases with distance from the magnet and is strongest at the poles.
For the compass method, describe marking the position of the needle tip, moving the compass so its tail is on that dot, and repeating.
To explain the Earth's magnetic core, link 'a compass points north even with no magnet nearby' to 'the Earth must have a magnetic field'.
summary: A magnetic field is where a magnet or magnetic material feels a force.
Field direction is the direction of the force on a north pole: N to S.
The field is strongest at the poles and weakens with distance.
Field lines closer together mean a stronger field.
A plotting compass can be used to map field lines.
Compasses point north because the Earth's core is magnetic.

questions.question: What is a magnetic field?
options: The material a magnet is made from
The point where a magnet is strongest
The region around a magnet where a force acts on a magnet or magnetic material
The current flowing through a magnet
markScheme: 1 mark: The region around a magnet where a force acts on a magnet or magnetic material
questions.explanation: A magnetic field is a region of space, around a magnet, in which magnetic forces act. The poles are where the field is strongest.

questions.explanation: Field lines show the direction of the force on a north pole, which is repelled by N and attracted to S, so they point from N to S.

questions.question: Where is the magnetic field around a bar magnet strongest?
options: In the middle of the magnet's side
markScheme: 1 mark: At the poles
questions.explanation: The field lines are most concentrated at the poles, so the field is strongest there.

questions.question: Which of these materials is NOT affected by a magnetic field?
markScheme: 1 mark: Copper
questions.explanation: Copper is not a magnetic material. Iron, steel, cobalt and nickel are all attracted by magnets.

questions.question: On a magnetic field diagram, how is a strong field shown?
markScheme: 1 mark: Lines drawn closer together
questions.explanation: Line spacing shows field strength: the closer the lines, the stronger the field. Line thickness has no meaning and lines never cross.

questions.question: What does a compass needle line up with?
options: The direction of the magnetic field
The direction of the force of gravity
markScheme: 1 mark: The direction of the magnetic field
questions.explanation: The needle is a small magnet, so its north pole points in the direction of the magnetic field at that point.

It lines up with the Earth's magnetic field

markScheme: 1 mark: It lines up with the Earth's magnetic field
questions.explanation: The Earth has a magnetic field produced by its core. The compass needle lines up with this field.

Both a north and a south pole

options: The fields cancel, so there is a neutral point with no resultant field
The field is very strong there
The field points from one north pole into the other
markScheme: 1 mark: The fields cancel, so there is a neutral point with no resultant field
questions.explanation: Each magnet's field points away from its N pole, so midway the two fields are equal and opposite and cancel, giving a neutral point. Field lines never cross.

questions.question: Define the direction of a magnetic field at a point.
markScheme: 1 mark: the direction of the force that would act on a north pole placed at that point
questions.explanation: This is the convention that sets field lines pointing from N to S.

questions.question: State two features of a correct field diagram for a bar magnet.
markScheme: 1 mark each for any two: arrows pointing from N to S; lines do not cross; lines closer together at the poles; lines further apart away from the magnet; smooth continuous curves from pole to pole
questions.explanation: Examiners look for direction, spacing and the rule that field lines never cross.

questions.question: State how the strength of the magnetic field changes as you move further from a bar magnet.
markScheme: 1 mark: it decreases (gets weaker)
questions.explanation: The field gets weaker with increasing distance from the magnet.

acceptedAnswers: dot at the tip of the needle
markScheme: 1 mark: place the compass near one pole of the magnet and mark the position of the needle's tip (north end) with a dot
1 mark: move the compass so the tail of the needle is on the dot and mark the new tip; repeat until the other pole is reached
1 mark: join the dots with a smooth line, add an arrow (N to S) and repeat from other starting points
questions.explanation: This method traces one line at a time; the compass needle always points along the field.

questions.question: Explain why the field lines around a bar magnet point away from the north pole.
markScheme: 1 mark: field direction is the direction of the force on a north pole
1 mark: a north pole is repelled by the magnet's north pole (like poles repel), so the force points away from it
questions.explanation: The definition of field direction plus 'like poles repel' gives the N to S direction.

questions.question: Explain how the behaviour of a magnetic compass provides evidence that the Earth's core is magnetic.
markScheme: 1 mark: a compass points north (lines up in a fixed direction) even when it is far from any magnet
1 mark: so there must be a magnetic field produced by the Earth (its core)
questions.explanation: A compass is a magnet that lines up with a field; with no nearby magnet the field must come from the Earth.

questions.question: A paper clip is held 2 cm from a magnet and then 10 cm from it. Compare the force on the paper clip in each position and explain the difference.
markScheme: 1 mark: the force is greater (stronger) at 2 cm
1 mark: because the magnetic field is stronger closer to the magnet
questions.explanation: Field strength decreases with distance, so the force on a magnetic material also decreases.

questions.question: Suggest why a compass is not reliable for finding north when it is used next to a steel car.
markScheme: 1 mark: steel is a magnetic material (it may be magnetised or become an induced magnet)
1 mark: the car's field (or the attraction) changes the direction the needle points, so it no longer lines up with the Earth's field alone
questions.explanation: Nearby magnetic materials distort the local field, so the compass shows the combined field rather than just the Earth's.

questions.question: A student plots the field of a bar magnet and finds the compass needle always points along the lines she has drawn. She then places a second bar magnet beside the first. Explain why her original field lines are no longer correct.
markScheme: 1 mark: the second magnet has its own magnetic field
1 mark: the two fields combine to give a different resultant field (in direction and strength)
1 mark: the compass now lines up with the combined field, so the field lines change shape
questions.explanation: Magnetic fields add together, so the pattern around two magnets differs from either alone.

questions.question: What is inside a magnetic compass that makes it work?
options: A coil carrying an electric current
A small bar magnet that can turn freely
markScheme: 1 mark: A small bar magnet that can turn freely
questions.explanation: The needle of a compass is a small bar magnet, free to rotate so it can line up with a magnetic field.

questions.question: Why do magnetic field lines never cross?
options: The field can only have one direction at any point
Field lines only exist inside magnets
markScheme: 1 mark: The field can only have one direction at any point
questions.explanation: If two lines crossed, the field would have two directions at the same point, which is impossible: a north pole there would feel only one resultant force.

questions.question: Describe the magnetic field pattern around a bar magnet. You may include a labelled sketch in your description.
markScheme: Indicative content: field lines leave the north pole and curve round to enter the south pole; arrows point from N to S; lines are closest together at the poles where the field is strongest; lines spread out further away where the field is weaker; lines never cross; pattern is symmetrical above and below the magnet; lines continue through the magnet from S to N.
Level 2 (3 to 4 marks): clear description including direction, variation of strength with distance and at least one other correct feature.
Level 1 (1 to 2 marks): some correct features, such as lines from N to S, without linking spacing to strength.
0 marks: no relevant content.
questions.explanation: A complete answer covers direction (N to S), strength (strongest at the poles, decreasing with distance) and the rules for drawing lines.

questions.question: Describe a method to plot the magnetic field pattern of a bar magnet using a plotting compass. Explain how the completed diagram shows where the field is strongest, and what the method suggests about the Earth.
markScheme: Indicative content: place the magnet on a sheet of paper on a bench away from other magnets and steel; draw round it and label the poles; place a plotting compass near the north pole; mark a dot at the tip of the needle; move the compass so its tail is on the dot and mark the new tip; repeat until the south pole is reached; join the dots with a smooth line and add an arrow N to S; repeat starting from several points around the poles; lines are closest together near the poles, showing the field is strongest there and weaker further away; before the magnet is placed, the compass points north, showing the Earth has a magnetic field (the core is magnetic); far from the magnet the compass lines up with the Earth's field.
Level 3 (5 to 6 marks): a detailed, logically ordered method that would produce a valid pattern, with a clear link between line spacing and strength and a valid point about the Earth's field.
Level 2 (3 to 4 marks): a workable method with some detail and some explanation of strength or the Earth's field.
Level 1 (1 to 2 marks): simple statements about using a compass or about the field being strong at the poles.
0 marks: no relevant content.
questions.explanation: The compass method traces lines dot by dot. Spacing of lines indicates strength. The fact that the compass points north with no magnet present is evidence of the Earth's magnetic field.

questions.question: A compass is placed at a point where the field of a bar magnet is much weaker than the Earth's magnetic field. Which way will it point?

markScheme: 1 mark: Approximately north, along the Earth's field
questions.explanation: The compass lines up with the resultant field. If the magnet's field is very weak at that point, the Earth's field dominates and the compass points roughly north.

questions.question: Name the type of force that acts between a magnet and a piece of iron.
markScheme: 1 mark: attraction (a non-contact force)
questions.explanation: The force between a magnet and a magnetic material is always attractive.

questions.question:
Figure 1 shows two bar magnets placed in a line with a north pole facing a south pole.
The gap between the magnets is 4 cm.
Describe and explain the magnetic field in the gap between the magnets.

markScheme: Indicative content: field lines go straight across the gap from the north pole to the south pole; lines are close together and roughly parallel, so the field in the gap is strong and nearly uniform; the two fields add in the same direction in the gap; unlike poles attract so the magnets would pull together; arrows point N to S.
Level 2 (3 to 4 marks): describes direction and strength with an explanation of why the fields add.
Level 1 (1 to 2 marks): simple description, such as lines go from N to S.
0 marks: no relevant content.
questions.explanation: Between unlike poles the two fields point the same way, giving a strong, nearly uniform field with straight, closely spaced lines from N to S.
